cards.explanation: The answer is the voice of the enemy. David, whose psalm this is, says he's distraught "…at the voice of the enemy, at the pressure of the wicked." It's people doing this to him, not a bug going around. He says they bring down disaster on him and resent him in their anger. I think anybody who has had someone's voice rattle around their head all day gets that.

The answer is False. David is not calm at all. He says, "My heart pounds within me, and the terrors of death assail me." Then he adds that fear and trembling grip him and horror has overwhelmed him. He doesn't dress it up, friends, and he says it straight to God.

The answer is wings like a dove. David says, "Oh, that I had wings like a dove!" He's not asking for a bigger sword. He's asking for a way out, because he says he would fly away and find rest. I think when you're that worn down, rest sounds better than any fight.
The answer is rest. David says that with wings like a dove he would "…fly away and find rest." He doesn't say he'd win anything or get anybody back. I think he's just tired all the way down.

The answer is the wilderness. David says, "In the wilderness I would remain." Not just a quick visit either, he says he would stay. Far from the noise is where he pictures rest. Then comes "Selah," and I'll let you sit with that picture a moment.

The answer is his shelter. David says, "I would hurry to my shelter, far from this raging tempest." Hurry is the word he picks, and it tells you how badly he wants a safe place. He calls what he's in a raging tempest. I think a shelter sounds mighty good in the middle of that.

The answer is that he sees violence and strife in the city. David gives his reason right in the verse: "…for I see violence and strife in the city." He's asking the Lord to confuse and confound their speech. The reason is what he sees happening around him. He doesn't hold it in, friends, he brings it to God.

The answer is False. The inside is no safer. David says, "Day and night they encircle the walls, while malice and trouble lie within." He adds, "Destruction is within…" and "oppression and deceit never leave the streets." So the trouble circles the walls, and it's inside too.

The answer is friend. David says, "But it is you, a man like myself, my companion and close friend." The word hits harder because of who it is. Right before this he says an enemy's insults he could endure. This one comes from someone close.

The answer is True. David says, "We shared sweet fellowship together; we walked with the crowd into the house of God." So they walked into the house of God together, with the crowd. That's a lot of shared road behind them. I think that's why the turn hurts so much.

The answer is that he calls to God. David says, "But I call to God, and the LORD saves me." Notice the "But." Everything before it is hurt and fear, and then he turns toward God. He doesn't pretend it's not hard, friends, he just takes it to the right place.

The answer is False. David says, "Morning, noon, and night, I cry out in distress, and He hears my voice." He cries out morning, noon and night, and he says God hears his voice. Nothing there says God gets tired of it.

The answer is that they don't change and have no fear of God. David says it's "…because they do not change and they have no fear of God." He names God as "…the One enthroned for the ages…" the One who hears. The reason is about who they are and how they treat God. Nothing else is added.

The answer is that his words sound kind but he means harm. David says, "His speech is smooth as butter, but war is in his heart." Then he says the words are "…softer than oil, yet they are swords unsheathed." So the voice sounds gentle while the heart means battle. Butter and oil, and still the blade is out.

The answer is upon the LORD. David says, "Cast your burden upon the LORD and He will sustain you…" Cast it means throw it, not set it down gently and keep a hand on it. Then he adds the promise that God will sustain you. Peter, one of Jesus' apostles, says something close: "Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you." (1 Peter 5:7)
The answer is False. David says, "He will never let the righteous be shaken." Never, not now and then. That promise comes right after he says the LORD will sustain you.

The answer is trust. David closes with "But I will trust in You." After the pounding heart, the violent city, and the friend who turned, he lands on trust. He doesn't say the trouble was small, friends. I think that's what makes the last line so strong.
